content: The Hirschberg test, also known as the Hirschberg corneal reflex test, is a diagnostic procedure used in ophthalmology and optometry to evaluate the presence of strabismus, which is a condition characterized by ocular misalignment. A photographic version of this test can also be employed to quantify the degree of strabismus. To perform the test, a light source is directed into the patient’s eyes, and the examiner observes the reflection of the light on the corneas. In individuals with normal ocular alignment, the light reflex is symmetrically positioned at the center of both corneas. However, in cases of abnormal ocular alignment, the position of the light reflex on the cornea can indicate the type of strabismus present. For example: In exotropia, where the affected eye is turned outward, the light reflex is observed on the medial aspect of the cornea. In esotropia, where the affected eye is turned inward, the light reflex is located on the lateral aspect of the cornea. In hypertropia, where the affected eye is positioned higher than the normal eye, the light reflex is seen on the inferior aspect of the cornea. In hypotropia, where the affected eye is positioned lower than the normal eye, the light reflex is found on the superior aspect of the cornea. A cover test can be used in conjunction with the Hirschberg test to determine the extent of esotropia or exotropia. It is also possible for an individual to present with multiple types of tropias simultaneously. For instance, in Graves' ophthalmopathy, it is not uncommon to observe esotropia caused by pathology of the medial rectus muscle coexisting with hypotropia due to pathology of the inferior rectus muscle. The Hirschberg test was developed by the German ophthalmologist Julius Hirschberg in 1886. He originally used a candle as the light source to observe the corneal light reflex in patients with strabismus.
